pool.prompt: A G.652.D fiber link is being budgeted at 1550 nm. Which attenuation value is most defensible to use when the actual cable datasheet is not yet available?
choices: 0.18 dB/km — the best vendor 'typical' figure seen in recent datasheets
0.22-0.25 dB/km — slightly above typical datasheet, leaving margin for aging and uncertainty
0.30 dB/km — the ITU-T G.652.D specification maximum
0.50 dB/km — a safe round conservative figure for any SMF
pool.explanation: 0.22-0.25 dB/km is the standard OSP designer planning value at 1550 nm. Using the 0.18 dB/km typical leaves no margin; using 0.30 dB/km (spec max) wastes headroom.
pool.citation: ITU-T G.652.D — attenuation coefficient <= 0.30 dB/km @ 1550 nm max; vendor datasheets typically show 0.18-0.22 dB/km.

pool.prompt: The G.652.D spec maximum at 1550 nm is <=0.30 dB/km, but typical production fiber measures 0.18-0.22 dB/km. Why is the spec maximum so much higher than what you actually get?
choices: Standards bodies deliberately inflate numbers
The spec maximum is the worst-case boundary for qualifying fiber — any fiber performing worse than this fails G.652.D; it's a rejection threshold, not a typical value
The 0.30 dB/km figure applies only to 1310 nm, not 1550 nm
Fiber attenuation increases over time, so the spec allows headroom for aging to 0.30 dB/km
pool.explanation: Spec maximums are quality thresholds, not typical performance targets. Production fiber is designed well inside the spec to ensure reliable manufacturing yield — the gap between spec-max and typical is a quality margin, not an error.

pool.prompt: What is the ITU-T G.652.D maximum attenuation coefficient across the 1310-1625 nm range, and specifically at 1550 nm?
choices: 0.4 dB/km across the whole range, including at 1550 nm
0.4 dB/km maximum generally (1310-1625 nm, incl. the 1383 nm water-peak), with a tighter 0.3 dB/km maximum specifically at 1550 nm
0.3 dB/km across the whole range, with no wavelength-specific variation
There is no defined maximum; only typical vendor values exist
pool.explanation: G.652.D specifies a general 0.4 dB/km maximum across most of the 1310-1625 nm range (including the 1383 nm water-peak region, which G.652.D specifically controls), with a tighter 0.3 dB/km maximum at the low-loss 1550 nm window.

pool.prompt: Why does an OSP designer use a 'designer planning value' for attenuation instead of just using the ITU-T spec maximum directly in every link budget?
choices: Because using the spec maximum is illegal under RUS rules

Because using the spec maximum in every calculation would make every budget look far worse than reality, potentially rejecting perfectly viable link distances — the planning value balances realistic margin against over-conservatism
Because the spec maximum only applies to multimode fiber
Because the planning value and spec maximum are numerically identical, making the distinction moot
pool.explanation: The planning value (slightly above typical, well below spec-max) leaves real margin for aging and procurement uncertainty without needlessly rejecting achievable link distances the way blindly using the worst-case spec number would.

pool.prompt: What does 7 CFR 1755.902 (the RUS minimum performance specification for fiber optic cables) require regarding attenuation test methods?
choices: It requires no specific test methodology — any vendor-chosen method is acceptable
It requires attenuation measurement per ANSI/ICEA S-87-640 Table 8.4, with single-mode optical performance compliant to ITU-T G.652 attribute tables, tested at 1310/1550 (and 1625 when specified) nm
It requires testing only at 850 nm, matching multimode standards
It applies exclusively to underground cable, not aerial
pool.explanation: 7 CFR 1755.902 ties RUS-funded fiber cable acceptance to ANSI/ICEA S-87-640's attenuation measurement methods (Table 8.4) and to ITU-T G.652 attribute compliance, with standard test wavelengths of 1310 and 1550 nm (1625 nm when the end user specifies it).
pool.citation: 7 CFR 1755.902 — Minimum performance Specification for fiber optic cables.

pool.prompt: A spec sheet says 'TIA-568 compliant' for connectors without specifying a revision or connector grade. What can you plan around using that information alone?
choices: A precise loss value of 0.25 dB per connector, since TIA-568 defines one universal number
The loss value is ambiguous — TIA-568 connector loss values differ across revisions and connector grades, so a revision-less citation is too vague to plan a link budget around
0.75 dB per connector, the highest historical TIA-568 value
Zero loss, since TIA-568-compliant connectors are lossless by definition
pool.explanation: TIA-568 connector loss values have changed across revisions and distinguish standard-grade from reference-grade connectors. Without a revision letter, the number is too vague for budget planning — the practical workaround is a tested loss certificate per connector/cord from the vendor.
pool.citation: TIA-568.3-D — confirm the specific revision against the edition adopted for your project.

pool.prompt: Between which two of the 'three numbers' framework values does the correct OSP link-budget planning value sit?
choices: Below the typical datasheet value and below the spec maximum
Above the typical datasheet value and below the spec maximum
Above the spec maximum, to be maximally conservative
Exactly equal to the spec maximum, for legal defensibility
pool.explanation: The designer planning value sits above the typical (real-world) datasheet value — to leave margin for aging, temperature, and uncertainty — but below the spec maximum, to avoid needless over-conservatism that would reject achievable link distances.

pool.prompt: Match each attenuation value at 1550 nm to its category in the 'three numbers' framework for G.652.D SMF.
pool.explanation: The spec maximum (<=0.30 dB/km) is the worst-case standard threshold. Typical datasheets show 0.18-0.22 dB/km. Designers plan around 0.22-0.25 dB/km — above typical to leave margin, well below spec-max to avoid over-conservatism.
pool.citation: ITU-T G.652.D (2024); vendor datasheets; OSP design practice.
